items.claim: The row's WEB quote spanning Prov.8.35 (“whoever finds me finds life” web:Prov.8.35) supplies no ketiv/qere disclosure, though 8:35 is a K/Q verse carrying the ketiv token inline before the qere.
items.evidence: MT Prov.8.35 reads the qere מֹ֭צְאִי immediately followed by the inline ketiv מצאי (verse_map_oshb.json), matching the inline-ketiv pattern the toolkit flags book-wide; pmarks_Prov.json lists Prov.8.35 in the kq inventory, and citation_sweep.py's own kq_web_quote_warn arm flags this exact row/quote pairing for missing K/Q disclosure. The boundary argument itself is independently strong and unaffected -- the petuchah at Prov.8.31 and Prov.8.36 double-anchors the seam, and the four-word summons opening Prov.8.32 is byte-identical to the opening of Prov.7.24 for its shared clause -- so this is a disclosure gap on the citation, not a defect in the seam warrant.

items.claim: The verbatim WEB quote for Prov.9.6 is delimited with straight quotes rather than the mandatory curly quotes paired with its inline web: ref.
items.evidence: The row's closing clause quotes WEB Prov.9.6 with a plain straight double quote pair rather than curly quotes, contrary to TOOLKIT.md's 'curly quotes for WEB text ONLY... straight quotes for everything else' and the campaign's 'curly quotes plus inline web: ref are MANDATORY at every layer' rule; check_web_quotes.py only pattern-matches curly-quoted spans, so this straight-quote instance evades the automated GREEN status. The quoted wording itself is a verbatim substring of verse_map_web.json Prov.9.6, and the underlying seam argument -- personified Wisdom as grammatical subject through 9:1-9:3 continuing into her own quoted invitation of 9:4-9:6, with the mode break at the participial 9:7 -- is byte-sound.

items.claim: Both verbatim WEB quotes in this row (near Prov.9.8 and Prov.9.9) use straight double quotes, and the Prov.9.8 quote also substitutes a straight apostrophe for the WEB source's own curly apostrophe.
items.evidence: The two English quotes bracketing the 9:7 participial maxim are both straight-quote-delimited rather than curly, the same convention gap as this cluster's other C1/ch.9 rows; the WEB source spells the first word as 'Don’t' with a curly apostrophe (verse_map_web.json Prov.9.8), so the row's plain apostrophe is not byte-identical to the text it claims to reproduce. Content is otherwise accurate (ellipsis-elided but verbatim), and the imperative-mood boundary argument (9:8-9:9 imperative core distinct from the nominal 9:10, petuchah at 9:9 correctly disclosed as single-witness) is sound.

items.claim: The verbatim WEB quote for Prov.9.11 is delimited with straight quotes rather than the mandatory curly quotes.
items.evidence: Same straight-quote delimiter gap as the row's neighbors in this cluster; the quoted clause is a verbatim substring of verse_map_web.json Prov.9.11 apart from lower-casing the sentence-initial word, an accepted mid-sentence-quoting convention and not a content error. The granularity call -- a nominal thesis (9:10) and first-person clause (9:11, recurring the personified voice of 9:1-9:6) closing on a conditional maxim (9:12), bracketed by the imperative unit before it and the new subject (foolish woman) after it -- is byte-grounded and unaffected by the delimiter defect.

items.claim: The verbatim WEB quote for Prov.9.16 is delimited with straight quotes rather than the mandatory curly quotes.
items.evidence: Same delimiter defect as the cluster's other ch.9 rows. The row's central literary claim is independently strong: the four-word consonantal opening מִי פֶ֭תִי יָסֻ֣ר הֵ֑נָּה of Prov.9.4 is byte-identical to the opening מִי פֶ֭תִי יָסֻ֣ר הֵ֑נָּה of Prov.9.16 (verse_map_oshb.json), a genuine mirror-invitation catchword tying Folly's call in 9:16 to Wisdom's own call in 9:4, correctly described as a match at the 'bare consonants' tier rather than over-claimed as fully pointed-byte-identical (the trailing words carry added vav-conjunctions in 9:16 that 9:4 lacks). The petuchah closing 9:18 is correctly disclosed as single-witness.

items.claim: Prov.10.1 is correctly held as a single single_proverb fusing the second (of exactly two) verse-initial mishle headers with its own antithetic bicolon, the C1/C2 seam corroborated by petuchah on both sides.
items.evidence: prov_device_inventory.json's collection_seams.mishle_verse_initial lists exactly Prov.1.1 and Prov.10.1 (count 2, object = verses whose first skeleton token is מִשְׁלֵ֗י), matching the row's claim precisely; pmarks_Prov.json marks both Prov.9.18 and Prov.10.1 PE, bracketing the collection seam the row cites as corroboration. Whole-verse span convention forecloses any sub-verse title/proverb split, and the rejected_alternative correctly names the live risk for this verse type (isolating the header from its own proverb body) rather than a strawman.

items.claim: The row's rejected_alternative overstates Prov.10.6's isolation from Prov.10.7, asserting they share 'nothing beyond the general righteous/wicked frame,' when a rare shared root links the two adjacent verses undisclosed.
items.evidence: sweep.py --skel (blessing root) returns exactly 8 verses book-wide: Prov.10.6, 10.7, 10.22, 11.11, 11.25, 11.26, 24.25, 28.20. Prov.10.6 (בְּ֭רָכוֹת, 'blessings') and Prov.10.7 (לִבְרָכָ֑ה, 'for a blessing') are two of those eight and are immediately adjacent (verse_map_oshb.json), sharing the same lexeme in different construct/prefixed forms -- exactly the class of byte-true device the campaign's cross-seam-cohesion rule requires disclosed before a row denies a neighbor connection. The row's own B-line evidence is independently confirmed: וּפִ֥י רְ֝שָׁעִ֗ים יְכַסֶּ֥ה חָמָֽס at Prov.10.6 is byte-identical to וּפִ֥י רְ֝שָׁעִ֗ים יְכַסֶּ֥ה חָמָֽס at Prov.10.11 (verse_map_oshb.json), so the single_proverb call for 10.6 is not necessarily wrong, but the 'high' confidence rests on an incomplete neighbor sweep that a digit-bearing check contradicts.

items.claim: The row's rejected_alternative states Prov.10.7 'does not continue into 10:6's head/mouth imagery' -- true for that specific image, but it omits a rarer shared root that does connect the two verses.
items.evidence: The same skeleton sweep (sweep.py --skel blessing-root, 8 verses book-wide) places Prov.10.6 and Prov.10.7 among only eight book-wide hits, adjacent to each other -- בְּ֭רָכוֹת ('blessings,' 10.6) and לִבְרָכָ֑ה ('for a blessing,' 10.7). The row's own memory/name argument for 10.7's content is byte-sound and its 10.7/10.8 boundary is clean (no shared root found there), so single_proverb likely still holds; the defect is the disclosure gap mirroring P05-010's -- both rows should name and refute the shared blessing-root rather than assert no connection to the other verse.
